newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: New York parking issue may go before UN Assembly.
newsitem.headline: New York parking issue may go before UN Assembly.

text.p: As New York City adopted tough new parking rules for diplomats on Tuesday, a U.N. committee threatened to take the issue to the 185-member General Assembly unless the United States met its concerns.
Rhetoric shifted into high gear as most committee members protested parts of the new regulations as a threat to international treaties on diplomatic immunity.
"Diplomatic immunity is like virginity," Jose Eduardo Martins Felicio of Brazil said. "Either you have it or you have not. I have not seen a half-virgin."

The committee will meet again on April 10 to take a decision if no new proposals were forthcoming from the United States in the intervening period. But judging from the debates, it has enough votes to call the assembly, in which all 185 U.N. members are represented, into an urgent session.
An assembly debate escalates the controversy but will not necessarily result in a change of the parking rules.

At issue are New York Mayor Rudolph Giuliani's new regulations that went into effect on Tuesday. They allow towing of foreign diplomats parked illegally and removal of their license plates if they fail to pay tickets within a year.

At the same time, each diplomatic mission, whether it has six employees or 100, would be guaranteed two parking spaces and one space outside the home of each ambassador living in Manhattan. Giuliani announced the regulations on March 10.
A special police "hot line" is being set up so that any unauthorised vehicles using those spots could be towed away.

But Felicio, in charge of political affairs at Brazil's U.N. mission, said none of the courtesies were working. He said he watched diplomatic cars being ticketed on Tuesday while being parked in their new legal spaces.
One policeman, he said, commented that, "It is not me who put the new sign there. I'm going to ticket the car anyway."
